newsitem.title: USA: U.S. debates ratifying chemical arms pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. debates ratifying chemical arms pact.

text.p: Both sides in the debate on an international treaty outlawing chemical weapons are bringing out their big guns in an effort to get it approved or defeated in the U.S. Senate by an April 29 deadline.

The Clinton administration is trying to pry the treaty from the grip of Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and win a two-thirds Senate vote before that date, when the treaty goes into force.
The 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, signed by more than 160 countries, bars states from acquiring, stockpiling, transferring or using chemical weapons.

Clinton says failure to ratify would mean the United States would have no role in implementing the pact and U.S. chemical companies could lose export trade to companies in countries that are parties to the treaties -- an argument also being made by the Chemical Manufacturers Association.
Helms on Saturday pledged to block the treaty from leaving his committee unless it is substantially modified, but administration officials have repeatedly said there is no prospect of amending it.

Prominent members of previous administrations are arguing about the treaty in newspaper articles as White House National Security Adviser Sandy Berger leads negotiations with a group of senators in an effort to pave the way to a Senate vote.

Opponents have been waging a vociferous campaign, asserting that compliance cannot be verified and the treaty will subject U.S. firms to unconstitutional searches by international inspectors or onerous red tape.

Supporters, including top administration officials, argue it will improve the ability of U.S. intelligence to monitor chemical threats to the United States and make it difficult for states like Libya to make poison gas.
In any case, they say, the United States is committed to destroying its own chemical weapons under a 1985 law; the treaty forces other countries to do the same.
This week a wordy debate in the public print continued with three former defence secretaries, James Schlesinger, Caspar Weinberger and Donald Rumsfeld, opposing the treaty.
They were replying to an article favouring ratification by former National Security Adviser Brent Scowcroft and former CIA Director John Deutch.

The administration seeks to answer all attacks in an effort to build public pressure for ratification, Arms Control and Disarmament Agency John Holum said on Friday. "We are finding a very receptive public response," he said.
The administration is taking heart from a recent Wirthlin poll showing that 84 percent of Democrats and Republicans questioned favoured ratification.
Behind the scenes, Berger and other officials are having talks with a group of nine Republican senators in an effort to defuse potentially fatal opposition in the Senate.
Helms, a North Carolina Republican, has often been a foe of arms agreements, has been waging a campaign against the chemical weapons convention and could bottle it up in committee.

"I have given the White House a long list of changes that must be made in this treaty before we agree to Senate ratification of it," Helms told the Conservative Political Action Conference, according to the Washington Post.
"I promise you this: Unless the administration makes the modifications I am demanding the (treaty) will not leave my committee. Period," he said.
Holum earlier declined to discuss details of the negotiations, but said "I feel fairly good" about the headway being made in the talks with senators.

Helms, backed by Republican Leader Trent Lott, has said that before the Senate deals with the treaty it should act on Republican agenda issues, such as restructuring the State Department and its agencies and legislation requiring United Nations reform and deployment of a national missile defence.

The treaty was before the Senate last September but was withdrawn at the administration's request when Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole opposed it, prompting fears it would not obtain the required two-thirds majority.
